patient.name: Sandra Whitfield
patient.complaint: First-ever seizure after three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting
background: Breast cancer 3 years ago: mastectomy, chemotherapy and trastuzumab
Told she was 'all clear' at her last check
Husband says she has been 'not herself' for a month

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a new seizure, headache or focal deficit in someone with known (or likely) cancer, often a lung, breast or melanoma primary, plus a lesion with oedema on CT.

points: Three weeks of headache, **worse on waking**, with vomiting.
Today: a **tonic-clonic seizure** in the supermarket.
Now awake and orientated, but tired.

steps.lead: Sandra's breast cancer is one of the big three primaries (**lung, breast, melanoma**) that spread to the brain.
A **known cancer** plus new headache or focal neurology is exactly when to suspect brain metastases in Sandra.

points: Husband noticed she has become irritable and forgetful.

steps.lead: Sandra has the raised ICP symptoms (morning headache, vomiting), a **seizure**, focal weakness and a **personality change**.

steps.q: What is the most likely cause of Sandra's seizure?
steps.r: A **new seizure in known cancer** is a brain metastasis until proven otherwise; papilloedema and focal weakness support a mass.

steps.lead: Sandra's CT confirms the signature: a small **solitary lesion** with oedema around it that looks out of proportion.

steps.title: Enhancing brain lesion: what is it?
head: Feature
Metastasis
Glioblastoma
Brain abscess
rows: White matter, can cross corpus callosum

steps.lead: Sandra's danger is worsening oedema: rising ICP, more seizures, **herniation** and a falling GCS.

visual.title: Sandra's GCS
visual.label: Sandra 15
visual.caption: Alert now. Any drop, a new dilated pupil or worsening vomiting means urgent escalation.

steps.text: A first seizure in a 59 year old with a cancer history is not 'new epilepsy'. **Image the brain** before labelling it.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (MRI brain with contrast; CT if unstable) and 'next investigation' to find the primary (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis).

steps.q: Sandra's first CT shows a lesion. Which scan best characterises it?
steps.r: **Contrast MRI** is the gold standard: it shows small or multiple lesions that CT misses.

steps.lead: Sandra is stable, so she has an urgent **MRI brain with contrast**; CT is for when MRI is unavailable or the patient is unstable.

points: MRI: **single** 2 cm enhancing lesion, right frontal lobe.

steps.title: Excluding metabolic causes of her seizure
steps.text: Normal sodium, calcium and glucose: the seizure is structural, not metabolic.

steps.lead: Sandra has a **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis** to stage her disease; a **biopsy** is needed if the primary is unknown or the lesion is atypical.

steps.title: Investigating suspected brain metastases
nodes: MRI brain with contrast (CT if unstable)
CT chest, abdomen, pelvis for primary or spread
Biopsy if primary unknown or diagnosis uncertain

steps.text: No known cancer and multiple lesions at the grey-white junction? **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis** to find the primary: lung is the commonest.
Do not perform a **lumbar puncture** with a mass lesion and papilloedema: risk of coning.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (dexamethasone for oedema) and 'definitive treatment' (surgery or stereotactic radiosurgery for limited disease; SRS, whole-brain radiotherapy or systemic therapy for multiple).

steps.q: Sandra has headache, vomiting and extensive oedema. What is first-line?
steps.r: **Dexamethasone** shrinks vasogenic oedema within days and relieves mass effect.

steps.lead: Sandra starts **dexamethasone** (with a PPI) to reduce her oedema and mass effect.

visual.title: Sandra on dexamethasone
visual.caption: Rapid relief within days: the steroid shrinks oedema, not the tumour.

steps.lead: Sandra's **seizure** is treated (levetiracetam started) and any sign of raised ICP means **urgent neurosurgical** escalation.

points: Neuro-oncology MDT: **single** lesion, no other disease on CT.
Good performance status: independent at home.
Told not to drive; she must inform the DVLA.

visual.title: How many metastases?
bands: single or limited: surgery or SRS
visual.label: Sandra 1
visual.caption: One lesion puts Sandra in the focal-treatment group.

steps.lead: Sandra's single lesion can be treated with **surgery or SRS**; with many lesions she would need SRS, whole-brain RT or systemic therapy.

steps.title: Definitive treatment decision
nodes: MDT: number, size, site, primary, fitness
Single or limited: surgery or SRS
Multiple: SRS, whole-brain RT or systemic therapy

steps.lead: Sandra's care follows the **NICE** brain tumours and metastases guidance: MDT decision, steroids for symptoms, focal treatment for limited disease.

steps.text: Dexamethasone treats **oedema**, not the cancer. Pick it for 'initial' management; pick SRS, surgery or radiotherapy for 'definitive'.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why metastases sit at the grey-white junction, why the oedema is so large (vasogenic), and how dexamethasone works.

steps.lead: Sandra's tumour cells travelled in the **arterial blood** and stuck where vessels narrow: the grey-white junction.

steps.title: From breast to brain
nodes: Carried in arterial circulation to the brain
Lodge at the grey-white junction (vessels narrow)

steps.lead: Sandra's 2 cm lesion has a huge rim of oedema because it breaks the **blood-brain barrier** and plasma leaks out.

steps.q: Why did Sandra's headache improve within a day of dexamethasone?
steps.r: Dexamethasone **reduces capillary permeability**, so oedema falls fast. The tumour itself is unchanged.

steps.lead: Sandra's quick improvement is the steroid sealing leaky capillaries, not shrinking the cancer.
Sandra's single lesion suits **SRS**: a focused dose that spares the brain around it. Many lesions would push towards whole-brain RT.

steps.text: Whole-brain radiotherapy costs more **neurocognitive** function, which is why focal SRS is preferred when lesions are few.

mcq.q: Which three primary cancers most commonly metastasise to the brain?
mcq.r: **Lung, breast and melanoma** (then renal and colorectal).

mcq.q: A new seizure in a patient with known cancer should raise suspicion of what?
Which headache feature suggests raised ICP?
o: Worse in the morning with vomiting
mcq.r: Morning headache with **vomiting** reflects raised ICP from oedema.

mcq.q: Which is a recognised complication of brain metastases?
mcq.r: Worsening oedema can cause **herniation** and reduced consciousness.
Urgent **MRI brain with contrast**; CT if MRI unavailable or patient unstable.

mcq.q: Which test looks for the primary tumour?
mcq.r: **CT CAP** finds the primary; biopsy gives tissue.

mcq.q: Which drug is first-line for symptomatic oedema?
mcq.r: **Dexamethasone** reduces vasogenic oedema and mass effect.

mcq.q: What is the definitive treatment for a single brain metastasis?
mcq.r: Single or limited disease: **surgery or SRS**.

mcq.q: Where do brain metastases preferentially lodge?
mcq.r: At the **grey-white junction**, where vessel calibre narrows.

mcq.q: Which type of oedema do brain metastases cause?
mcq.r: **Vasogenic** oedema from a disrupted blood-brain barrier.

points.why: Commoner than primary brain tumours in adults.

points.p: Lung (commonest)
points.why: Smoker in the stem: think lung.

points.p: Breast

prompts.q: Why do metastases sit at the grey-white junction and cause so much oedema?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: haematogenous spread and a broken blood-brain barrier.

points.p: Haematogenous arterial spread lodges where vessel calibre narrows
Tumour disrupts the blood-brain barrier: plasma leaks (vasogenic oedema)
points.why: Oedema out of proportion to size.

prompts.q: How does dexamethasone work, and why SRS for few lesions but whole-brain RT for many?

points.p: Dexamethasone stabilises the blood-brain barrier, reducing capillary permeability
SRS: focused high dose that spares surrounding tissue
Whole-brain RT treats diffuse disease but causes more neurocognitive side effects

glossary.Brain metastases: Secondary cancer deposits in the brain that have spread from a primary tumour elsewhere.
glossary.Primary: The original tumour from which secondary deposits spread.
glossary.Melanoma: Skin cancer of pigment cells that frequently spreads to the brain.
glossary.Mass effect: Pressure from a lesion pushing on and displacing surrounding brain.
glossary.Vasogenic oedema: Brain swelling from plasma leaking through a damaged blood-brain barrier, typical around tumours.
glossary.Cytotoxic oedema: Swelling of brain cells themselves from energy failure, as in stroke; steroids do not help it.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: Tight junctions in brain capillaries that stop most substances leaking from blood into brain tissue.
glossary.ICP: Intracranial pressure: the pressure inside the skull.
glossary.Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic discs from raised intracranial pressure.
glossary.Pronator drift: When an arm held out palm-up drifts down and turns inwards, a sign of subtle upper motor neurone weakness.
glossary.Grey-white matter junction: The boundary between the cortex and the underlying white matter, where metastases typically lodge.
glossary.Haematogenous spread: Spread of tumour cells through the bloodstream.
glossary.Herniation: Brain tissue being pushed across rigid structures inside the skull by raised pressure, which can be fatal.
glossary.Coning: Herniation of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the brainstem.
glossary.GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, a 3 to 15 score of eye, verbal and motor responses.
glossary.Ataxia: Unsteady, uncoordinated movement, often from a cerebellar lesion.
glossary.Visual field deficit: Loss of part of the field of vision, such as a homonymous hemianopia.
glossary.Homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, from a lesion behind the optic chiasm.
glossary.Tonic-clonic seizure: A generalised seizure with stiffening then rhythmic jerking of the limbs.
glossary.Dexamethasone: Potent corticosteroid that rapidly reduces vasogenic oedema around brain tumours.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, given with high-dose steroids to protect the stomach.
glossary.Levetiracetam: Anti-epileptic drug commonly used for seizures caused by brain tumours.
glossary.SRS: Stereotactic radiosurgery: a single precise, high-dose beam aimed at a small target, sparing surrounding brain.
glossary.Stereotactic radiosurgery: Highly focused high-dose radiotherapy to a small target such as a single metastasis.
glossary.WBRT: Whole-brain radiotherapy: radiation to the entire brain for multiple metastases.
glossary.Whole-brain radiotherapy: Radiation to the whole brain, used for numerous metastases, at a cost to memory and cognition.
glossary.Systemic anti-cancer treatment: Drugs that act throughout the body, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy.
glossary.Neurocognitive: Relating to thinking, memory and concentration.
glossary.CT CAP: CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, used to find a primary tumour or other spread.
glossary.Biopsy: Taking a tissue sample to confirm the type of cancer under the microscope.
glossary.MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting where specialists agree a treatment plan.
glossary.Performance status: A score of how well a patient functions day to day, used to decide if they can tolerate treatment.
glossary.Glioblastoma: The most aggressive primary brain tumour in adults, usually a single irregular ring-enhancing mass.
glossary.Meningioma: A usually benign tumour of the meninges, attached to the dura, outside the brain tissue.
glossary.Trastuzumab: Antibody treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer, which crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly.
glossary.DVLA: UK Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which patients must tell after a seizure or brain tumour diagnosis.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man who was treated for lung cancer 18 months ago has a generalised seizure at home. For the past 2 weeks he has had headaches on waking and has vomited twice. He has mild right arm weakness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. A CT head shows a small solitary left parietal lesion with extensive surrounding oedema.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis: new seizure plus a lesion on CT.

clues: small solitary left parietal lesion with extensive surrounding oedema
steps.x: Known cancer, raised ICP symptoms, contralateral weakness, small lesion with disproportionate oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain metastasis** from his lung primary.

elim: No alcohol history, and there is a structural lesion on CT.
No fever or infective source.
Idiopathic epilepsy does not cause a focal lesion or focal weakness.
A meningioma is dural-based, slow and usually has little oedema.

steps.x: **C. Brain metastasis.** Rule: new seizure + known cancer = metastasis until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 57 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer has a 3 week history of headache and new clumsiness of her left hand. She is alert and stable. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. A non-contrast CT head shows an area of oedema in the right parietal lobe but no clear lesion.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: The diagnostic test for the brain lesion itself.

clues: new clumsiness of her left hand
steps.x: Suspected metastasis; CT is inconclusive; she is stable enough for MRI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MRI brain with contrast**, the gold standard.

elim: CT CAP stages the body; it does not characterise the brain lesion.
EEG does not show structural lesions.
LP is unsafe with oedema and a possible mass.
Skull X-ray cannot see brain tissue.

steps.x: **D. MRI brain with contrast.** Rule: stable = MRI; unstable = CT.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with known metastatic lung cancer has 5 days of worsening headache and vomiting. An MRI shows three metastases with marked surrounding oedema. He is alert. His pulse rate is 84 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of symptomatic oedema.
Raised ICP symptoms from vasogenic oedema in a stable patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dexamethasone** to reduce oedema and mass effect.

elim: Furosemide does not treat vasogenic oedema.
Mannitol is a short-term bridge for impending herniation, not first-line here.
He has not had a seizure; levetiracetam does not treat oedema.
Radiotherapy is definitive treatment, decided by the MDT later.

steps.x: **A. Dexamethasone.** Rule: oedema around metastases = steroid first.

technique.stem: A 54 year old woman with melanoma has an MRI showing four small enhancing lesions, each at the junction of the cortex and underlying white matter. She has no fever. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason the lesions are found at this site?

steps.x: A mechanism: why the grey-white junction?

clues: junction of the cortex and underlying white matter
steps.x: Multiple metastases at the grey-white junction: haematogenous spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Arterial emboli of tumour cells lodge where **vessel calibre narrows**.

elim: Skull invasion gives a single lesion next to bone.
The brain has no conventional lymphatic route for metastasis.
Perineural spread follows nerves, not the grey-white junction.
CSF spread gives leptomeningeal disease, coating the surface.

steps.x: **C. Narrowing of vessel calibre.** Rule: haematogenous spread lodges at the grey-white junction.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has 3 weeks of headache, weight loss and haemoptysis. Today he had a first seizure. He has mild left-sided weakness. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources). CT head shows a single right frontal lesion with surrounding oedema.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right upper zone mass with right hilar enlargement.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A heavy smoker with haemoptysis, weight loss and a lung mass now has a seizure and a brain lesion with oedema: a metastasis from lung cancer, the commonest primary.

steps.x: A diagnosis: link the chest X-ray to the brain lesion.

clues: single right frontal lesion with surrounding oedema
steps.x: Likely lung cancer (mass on CXR) plus a brain lesion with oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain metastasis** from a lung primary.

elim: An AVM presents with haemorrhage or seizures in younger people, without a lung mass.
No fever or infective source.
Glioblastoma would not explain the lung mass and haemoptysis.
Meningioma is dural-based, slow and unrelated to the lung.

steps.x: **C. Brain metastasis.** Rule: lung mass + brain lesion = lung primary with metastasis.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has 2 weeks of headache and confusion. His wife says a mole on his back changed shape and bled last year but he never had it checked. MRI shows multiple enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction, some containing blood. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely primary tumour?
practice.e: A changing, bleeding mole with multiple haemorrhagic brain metastases points to melanoma, one of the three commonest primaries. Basal cell carcinoma almost never metastasises.

steps.x: Which primary caused these brain metastases?

clues: mole on his back changed shape and bled
steps.x: A suspicious mole and haemorrhagic metastases.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Melanoma**.

elim: BCC is locally invasive and very rarely metastasises.
Cutaneous SCC spreads to lymph nodes, rarely to brain.
Prostate cancer spreads to bone, rarely to brain.
Thyroid carcinoma is not a common brain primary and there is no neck lump.

steps.x: **C. Melanoma.** Rule: lung, breast and melanoma are the big three.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with treated breast cancer has 3 weeks of headache and keeps walking into objects on her left side. MRI shows a single enhancing lesion with oedema in the right occipital lobe. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg and GCS 15.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: A right occipital metastasis damages the right visual cortex, which receives the left visual field from both eyes: left homonymous hemianopia.

steps.x: An examination finding from a lesion site.

clues: walking into objects on her left side
steps.x: Right visual cortex lesion; she misses things on the left.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Left homonymous hemianopia**.

elim: Bitemporal loss is from the chiasm, e.g. pituitary tumour.
A central scotoma is from optic nerve or macular disease.
Right-sided field loss needs a left-sided lesion.
An RAPD is an optic nerve sign, not occipital.

steps.x: **C. Left homonymous hemianopia.** Rule: occipital lesion = opposite field in both eyes.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with metastatic lung cancer has 10 days of headaches that are worst on waking, with vomiting. He is drowsy but rousable and has bilateral papilloedema. His pulse rate is 62 bpm, BP 164/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
o: Brain metastases with raised intracranial pressure
practice.e: Morning headache, vomiting, drowsiness and papilloedema with normal sodium and calcium point to raised ICP from brain metastases with vasogenic oedema.

steps.x: Cause of a drowsy patient with lung cancer: structural or metabolic?
Raised ICP features (papilloedema, relative bradycardia, high BP); metabolic labs normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain metastases** causing raised ICP.

elim: Calcium is normal.
Sodium is normal.
Opioid toxicity causes pinpoint pupils and slow breathing, not papilloedema.
SVCO causes facial swelling and distended neck veins, not papilloedema with focal headache pattern.

steps.x: **A. Brain metastases with raised ICP.** Rule: papilloedema with normal metabolic labs = structural.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with known brain metastases from breast cancer becomes rapidly more drowsy over 2 hours. Her GCS falls from 14 to 9 and her right pupil is now fixed and dilated. Her pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 188/96 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her deterioration?
practice.e: Falling GCS, a fixed dilated pupil and Cushing's response (bradycardia, hypertension, slow breathing) mean herniation from worsening raised ICP, a recognised complication of brain metastases.

steps.x: A complication: why is she deteriorating?

clues: pulse rate is 52 bpm, BP 188/96 mmHg
steps.x: Third nerve compression plus Cushing's triad: herniation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transtentorial (uncal) herniation**.

elim: Horner syndrome gives a small pupil with ptosis.
Myasthenic crisis causes weakness and respiratory failure, not a fixed dilated pupil.
Opioids cause pinpoint pupils.
Syncope is brief, with recovery.

steps.x: **D. Transtentorial herniation.** Rule: fixed dilated pupil + falling GCS = herniation; escalate now.

practice.stem: A 48 year old woman who had breast cancer treated 5 years ago has had a first focal seizure with jerking of her right hand. She has had 2 weeks of morning headaches. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. MRI shows two small enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction, each with oedema out of proportion to its size.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A cancer history, new seizure, and multiple lesions at the grey-white junction with disproportionate oedema are classic brain metastases, even years after treatment.

steps.x: A diagnosis with an MRI description.

clues: two small enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction
oedema out of proportion to its size
steps.x: Past cancer, new seizure, multiple lesions in the classic site.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Brain metastases**.

elim: No fever or source; abscesses are usually solitary.
CVST gives venous infarcts or haemorrhage, not enhancing lesions.
Meningioma is dural-based and usually single.
MS plaques are periventricular without large oedema in a 48 year old with cancer.

steps.x: **B. Brain metastases.** Rule: breast cancer can relapse in the brain years later.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with known metastatic lung cancer is brought in after a seizure. He remains drowsy, with a GCS of 9, and is vomiting. His pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 170/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% on 2 L/min oxygen.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: MRI with contrast is the gold standard, but in an unstable patient with GCS 9 and signs of raised ICP, CT head is quicker and safer to do first.

steps.x: Initial investigation: is the patient stable enough for MRI?

clues: pulse rate is 58 bpm, BP 170/94 mmHg
steps.x: Unstable, possible raised ICP: speed matters.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT head** now; MRI later when stable.

elim: EEG does not show a mass or bleed.
LP with raised ICP risks coning.
MRI is the gold standard but unsafe and slow in an unstable patient.
PET-CT is for staging, not emergencies.

steps.x: **A. CT head.** Rule: MRI if stable; CT if unavailable or unstable.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with no known cancer has 4 weeks of headache and word-finding difficulty. She has lost 6 kg. MRI brain shows three enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction with surrounding oedema. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Multiple lesions at the grey-white junction with weight loss suggest metastases from an unknown primary: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis looks for it. Biopsy follows if needed.

steps.x: Next investigation after the MRI: find the primary.

clues: three enhancing lesions at the grey-white matter junction
steps.x: Likely metastases with no known primary.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis**.

elim: Bone marrow biopsy is for haematological malignancy.
LP is unsafe with mass lesions and oedema.
Tumour markers are non-specific and do not localise a primary.
Spine MRI is for cord compression symptoms, which she does not have.

steps.x: **B. CT CAP.** Rule: unknown primary = CT CAP, then biopsy.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with lung cancer has 1 week of worsening headache and nausea. CT head shows a 2 cm lesion in the left parietal lobe with extensive surrounding oedema. He is alert. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 140/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Dexamethasone is first-line for symptomatic vasogenic oedema around a metastasis, relieving mass effect within days. Radiotherapy is decided later by the MDT.

steps.x: Initial management of symptomatic oedema.
Vasogenic oedema causing raised ICP symptoms; stable.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dexamethasone**.

elim: Analgesia alone ignores the cause of the headache.
Hypertonic saline is for acute herniation, not an alert patient.
Aciclovir treats HSV encephalitis.
Radiotherapy is definitive, not initial, management.

steps.x: **B. Dexamethasone.** Rule: initial = steroid for oedema.

practice.stem: A 56 year old woman with breast cancer, whose body disease is well controlled, has a single 1.5 cm metastasis in a deep part of the left thalamus on MRI. She is fully independent. Her symptoms have settled on dexamethasone. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
practice.e: A single small metastasis in a fit patient needs focal treatment. Its deep site makes surgery hazardous, so stereotactic radiosurgery is best; whole-brain RT is for multiple lesions.

steps.x: Definitive treatment: count the lesions and check the site.

clues: deep part of the left thalamus
steps.x: Single, small, deep lesion in a fit patient with controlled disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Stereotactic radiosurgery**.

elim: Steroids only treat oedema and cause long-term harm.
She is fit with treatable disease.
Systemic therapy alone is for multiple metastases.
Whole-brain RT is for multiple lesions and harms cognition.

steps.x: **C. SRS.** Rule: single or limited = surgery or SRS; deep = SRS.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with small cell lung cancer has MRI showing more than 20 metastases throughout both cerebral hemispheres. His headaches have improved on dexamethasone. He walks independently. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for his brain disease?
o: Stereotactic radiosurgery to the largest lesion
practice.e: More than 20 metastases are too many for focal treatment: whole-brain radiotherapy treats disease throughout the brain, at the cost of more neurocognitive side effects.

steps.x: Treatment for many metastases.
Diffuse disease in a fit patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Whole-brain radiotherapy**.

elim: Surgery is for single, accessible lesions.
Intrathecal chemotherapy is for leptomeningeal disease.
He is fit and symptomatic; treatment is appropriate.
Treating one lesion leaves the other 19 untreated.

steps.x: **E. Whole-brain radiotherapy.** Rule: too many for SRS = whole-brain RT.

practice.stem: A 59 year old woman with lung cancer has a 1 cm metastasis in the right frontal lobe surrounded by a large area of oedema extending through the white matter. Her symptoms improve within 24 hours of dexamethasone. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the oedema?
o: Disruption of the blood-brain barrier with plasma leakage
practice.e: Tumour cells disrupt the blood-brain barrier, so plasma leaks out: vasogenic oedema, often out of proportion to the lesion and responsive to dexamethasone.

steps.x: A mechanism: why so much oedema around a small lesion?

clues: large area of oedema extending through the white matter
steps.x: Small lesion, big white matter oedema, steroid-responsive: vasogenic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood-brain barrier disruption** with plasma leakage.

elim: Cytotoxic oedema is from ischaemia and does not respond to steroids.
Interstitial oedema is periventricular, from hydrocephalus.
No hyponatraemia is given; osmotic oedema is diffuse.
Nothing suggests sinus thrombosis.

steps.x: **B. BBB disruption.** Rule: tumour oedema = vasogenic = steroid-responsive.
